Judging from some of the  speeches lately from Fed officials, it looks like too-big-to-fail is—they view this as the next step  where attention should be paid and work should be done.
I believe that too-big-to-fail was an important cause,  or at least a propagating mechanism, of the financial crisis.
And I believe it’s absolutely  incumbent upon us to do all we can to eliminate too-big-to-fail.
Now, obviously, the complexity and the international aspects of these firms make that a  much more challenging task, but I think we’re making progress there.

And, indeed,  part of the reason that there’s been some downgrade or potential downgrade for some U.S.  financial institutions is the judgment of the ratings agencies that the so-called implicit  government support that these institutions have is less than in the past.
And, you know, we’ve seen, for example, less volatility in  interest rates related to greater certainty about what the Fed is likely to do.
And do you believe that you are at an equivalent degree of monetary accommodation  today using your unconventional tools?
I don’t want to cite a particular number, but it probably would be negative.
That doesn’t mean we  might not take further action; we are certainly prepared to take further action.
And on the other side, as I was  saying earlier, if we can safely unwind a failing firm, then we no longer have too-big-to-fail,  obviously, and so I think that’s a very, very important objective.
So we will take actions based on those economic objectives and not try  to achieve certain market outcomes.
Of course, we’ll continue to monitor the situation, and if we believe that financial  conditions for whatever reason are inconsistent with our macroeconomic objectives, then we will  act to fix that.

But, again, our expectation is that, at whatever point that the purchases end, that  financial markets being quite forward looking will have anticipated that, and that the effects  ought to be moderate.
Now, of course, Japan had a much bigger bubble and a much bigger shock when the bubble  collapsed, and so these differences may be certainly understandable.
